title: The Blind Spot in Orbit: Why Space Could Be the Next Infrastructure Crisis
summary: Are organisations becoming so reliant on third party space assets that they would face severe disruption if the assets were impacted by a cyber attack?
body_markdown:
[Cybersecurity](https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/blog/category/cybersecurity/)


[Points of View](https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/blog/category/points-of-view/)


*Are organisations becoming so reliant on third party space assets that they would face severe disruption if the assets were impacted by a cyber attack?*


When most people think of space technology, they imagine routine weather forecasts or blue-dot navigation on a smartphone map. But behind those quiet satellite signals lies an invisible digital thread holding modern society together. From crop harvesting schedules to international flight routes and supermarket supply chains, daily life on Earth is deeply dependent on data from space.


Yet space security remains the cyber risk that very few in executive boardrooms are addressing. As the space economy surges toward a


[$1.01 trillion valuation by 2034](https://nova.space/press-release/global-space-economy-reaches-626-billion-marking-a-new-phase-of-growth/) , a dangerous blind spot has emerged. Cyber threats to orbital infrastructure are no longer a theoretical hazard—they are happening now.


## Privatization Outpacing Security


Historically, space operations were the exclusive domain of governments operating in strictly air-gapped environments with near-zero tolerance for risk. Today, rapid commercial privatization has slashed launch costs, but speed to market is dangerously outstripping security by design. Commercial operators inherit standard enterprise IT vulnerabilities, complex supply chain risks, unpatched APIs, and operational technology gaps.


The systemic disconnect is stark:


- According to data from the


[Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/the-space-economy-at-a-glance-2026_cbf9b240-en.html) , space-based systems now


**support more than 50% of all critical services and infrastructure** across modern economies.


- [The European Commission’s latest assessment](https://commission.europa.eu/topics/space_en) is that


**10% of the EU’s GDP is enabled directly or indirectly by satellite navigation signals** . This equates to around €1.88 trillion based on the EU’s GDP for 2025.


- Yet


**85% of organisations** aren’t factoring space assets into their cyber risk mitigation strategy,


[according to the World Economic Forum](https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-cybersecurity-outlook-2026/) .


## Physical Consequences on the Ground


Unlike typical corporate breaches, orbital cyber attacks can trigger immediate physical impacts on Earth. Tampering with satellite telemetry can destabilize regional crop yields by altering planting schedules or paralyze commercial aviation by injecting false data into flight-navigation networks.


Crucially, these risks are not limited to assets in orbit. Ground-based power substations, telemetry command hubs, and downlink facility infrastructure have become primary cyber-physical targets. A coordinated cyber attack on local energy substations supporting satellite ground operations could sever communication links and ground control just as effectively as an in-orbit compromise.


[A study commissioned by the European Space Agency (ESA)](https://www.esa.int/Applications/Connectivity_and_Secure_Communications/What_would_happen_without_satellite_communications) modeled the impact of a hypothetical


**7-day satellite communications outage** across ESA member states and Canada. The potential cost reaches


**up to €20 billion ($21.8 billion) in total economic losses** . This includes


**€19 billion** in maritime logistics and port bottlenecks,


**€558 million** in direct aviation losses (canceling ~4,000 transatlantic flights),


**€352 million** in lost connectivity for emergency services and remote communities, and


**€89.8 million** from stalled offshore energy operations.


## Aging Tech Meets Advanced Threat Actors


Geostationary satellites carry mission lifespans of 10 to 15 years, locking critical communications into legacy hardware designed before modern cyber threats existed. Nation-states and cybercriminals are exploiting these gaps; Palo Alto Networks


**Unit 42 threat intelligence** currently tracks multiple state-sponsored groups actively targeting space-sector systems.


## What Leaders Must Do Now


Governments and enterprise boards must recognize space-based timing, navigation, and observation as


**core national critical infrastructure** . Leadership teams should execute four priorities immediately:


1. **Map Space Dependencies:** Audit third-party services, cloud links, and automated logistics relying on satellite telemetry.


2. **Establish Terrestrial Backups:** Build manual redundancies—including ground-based radio networks and offline inventory controls—for scenario planning when space signals go dark.


3. **Elevate Supply Chain Audits:** Evaluate whether key vendors rely on single-point-of-failure commercial satellite constellations or unfortified ground substations.


4. **Update Risk Registers:** Formally integrate space dependencies into corporate cyber risk registers.


Translating these action items into real-world operational resilience requires moving beyond static compliance policies. To protect complex ecosystems—where ground stations, power substations, cloud environments, and orbital data streams converge—organizations need a unified, platformized approach to security that provides continuous visibility across every link in the space supply chain.


In the modern threat landscape, business resilience, national sovereignty, and space security are inseparable. It is time for leaders to look up before an orbital breach brings ground operations to a standstill.
